fetched_contents.text: Influence of electrospinning parameters on the development of high-quality electrospun nanofibers: A brief critical assessment 1. Introduction The biomedical applications in tissue engineering heavily depend on the properties of scaffolds, including biocompatibility, osteoconductivity, degradability, high surface area-to-volume ratios, and mechanical strength [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. Among various manufacturing techniques used to create nanofiber scaffolds, including phase separation, self-assembly, electrospinning, melt-blowing, and template synthesis, the electrospinning technique stands out for its ability to produce implants with diverse layer characteristics. This technique offers significant advantages for developing scaffolds with complex micro and macro morphology [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], as well as in soft tissue engineering Soft tissue is seen as a crucial component of the human body, connecting and supporting various structures and organs [11], which encompasses skeletal muscles, tendons, blood vessels, ligaments, nerves, cardiac patches, fibrous tissues, and synovial membranes [12], and a damage to such soft tissue has been a common medical issue that causes pain for many patients in general. Therefore, to promote tissue regeneration, it is essential to produce high-quality scaffolds that can be used to effectively repair and enhance the regeneration of soft tissues [4], [5]. High-quality electrospun nanofibers for tissue engineering are nanoscale fibers created using the electrospinning technique. These fibers possess optimized physical, chemical, and biological properties that closely mimic the extracellular matrix (ECM), which supports and enhances cell adhesion, proliferation, differentiation, and tissue regeneration. They are characterized by their uniform fiber morphology, biocompatibility, suitable mechanical strength, high porosity, controlled biodegradability, and surface functionality tailored to meet the specific requirements of target tissues, such as bone, skin, and nerve. Similarly, high-quality electrospun nanofibers for drug delivery are nanoscale fiber structures produced using the electrospinning technique. These nanofibers effectively encapsulate, protect, and release therapeutic agents in a controlled and targeted manner. They feature uniform morphology, a high surface area, biocompatibility, adjustable porosity, and customizable drug release profiles, making them ideal carriers for delivering drugs to specific tissues or organs. For example, the electrospinning technique has significantly impacted soft tissue regeneration due to the unique material composition and structural properties of electrospun nanofibers [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]. This technique can also be utilized to produce nanofiber matrices, including drawing, molecular self-assembly, freeze-drying, phase separation, and electrospinning [16], [17]. Additionally, electrospinning has emerged as a simple and reproducible technique for fabricating polymeric nanofiber matrices from both solutions and melts [18], [19]. Although electrospun nanofiber matrices have been studied as scaffolds used in tissue engineering, however, their properties could only influence cellular behavior [20]. The electrospinning technique that involves pumping a polymer solution through a needle tip situated at a specific distance from a grounded or oppositely charged collector has been used to effectively produce nanofibrous non-wovens from various materials, as illustrated in Fig. 1. On the other hand, electrospun nanofiber scaffolds are more recognized as better technology with great potential for various biomedical applications, including biosensing, drug delivery, and the repair and regeneration of soft and hard tissues, as well as wound healing [9], [10], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]. Despite the ease and acceptable usage of this technique, there is a notable gap in research about some significant effects of the different combinations of electrospinning parameters on various fabrications of electrospun nanofibers [27]. A study by Manoukian et al. [28] highlighted the effectiveness of the electrospinning technique, which enhances the production of high-quality polymer nanofiber scaffolds suitable for soft tissue regeneration (see Fig. 2). However, adjusting electrospinning parameters in their study could only strengthen the physicochemical properties of nanofiber matrices towards specific requirements of some applications. Concentration has a central role in electrospinning because it determines solution viscosity, which in turn controls jet behavior and fiber morphology. The evidence here suggests that higher polymer concentrations increase solution viscosity, with one source noting that “higher polymer concentrations resulted in larger solution viscosity, suggesting that more entanglement couplings led to thicker electrospun ...” [N2-R1]. Another source states that for PVP, “the viscosity and fiber diameter decrease with decreasing concentration of PVP in the electrospinning solution” [N2-R2]. This is consistent with the broader conclusion that concentration is a key rheological parameter affecting electrospinning performance [N5-R3].

Regarding the concentration range where jet breakup or dripping transitions occur, the evidence is indirect but informative. The review material explicitly states that the rheology of the spinning fluid greatly influences jet stability and morphology [N4-R1]. It also connects solution concentration to fiber morphology and notes that concentration and viscosity are among the dominant factors influencing fiber diameter and morphology [N4-R2]. A separate source adds that polymer concentration and viscosity are a predominant factor influencing morphology and diameter [N4-R4]. While the evidence does not provide a specific numerical threshold for the transition point, it clearly supports the idea that concentration changes can move the system between stable jetting, breakup, and dripping regimes.

Higher concentration increases solution viscosity and resistance to jet stretching because the more concentrated solution becomes more viscous, which reduces the ease with which the jet can elongate under the applied electric field. The same source notes that higher polymer concentrations resulted in larger solution viscosity [N2-R1]. Another source emphasizes that viscosity is a vital material parameter for electrospinning [N5-R3]. This means that at higher concentrations, the solution is harder to stretch into a thin jet, which can stabilize the jet initially but also make it more prone to breakup if the viscosity becomes too high. The review material also links rheology to fiber morphology and fiber diameter, reinforcing that viscosity and concentration are tightly coupled in determining the final structure [N4-R1].

On fiber diameter, beading, and alignment, the evidence points to a clear trade-off. Higher viscosity can reduce fiber diameter in some regimes because it promotes elongation and suppresses bead formation, but the same source also says that lower PVP concentration leads to lower viscosity and lower fiber diameter, suggesting that the relationship is not monotonic [N2-R2]. A separate review source notes that molecular weight, alongside concentration and viscosity, is a predominant factor influencing morphology and diameter [N4-R4]. Another source states that high surface tension inhibits electrospinning, leading to instability with an increased tendency for the jet to break, resulting in beaded fibers [N6-R3]. This implies that concentration indirectly affects beading through its effect on viscosity and surface tension. The evidence also supports that concentration affects alignment, since morphology is influenced by the spinning fluid’s rheology [N4-R1]. In sum, concentration affects fiber diameter by controlling viscosity, surface tension, and the stability of the jet, while beading and alignment depend on how well the jet can stretch, charge, and deposit evenly [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R1][N4-R4].

## Integrated final answer: how concentration and viscosity affect jet stability and nanofiber morphology

### 1. General principle: concentration sets the baseline for jet behavior and morphology

Concentration is a central factor in electrospinning because it determines solution viscosity, which in turn controls jet behavior and fiber morphology [N2-R1][N5-R3]. Higher polymer concentration generally increases solution viscosity, while lower concentration reduces viscosity and may lower fiber diameter [N2-R1][N2-R2]. This means that concentration is not only a rheological parameter, but also a key determinant of whether the jet remains stable, breaks up, or transitions to dripping [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

The evidence does not provide a precise numerical threshold for the transition point between jet breakup and dripping, but it clearly supports the idea that concentration changes can shift the system between stable jetting, breakup, and dripping regimes [N4-R1][N4-R2]. At the same time, higher concentration can increase resistance to jet stretching because the solution becomes more viscous and harder to elongate under the electric field [N2-R1][N5-R3].

### 2. Viscosity determines how the jet elongates, charges, and fragments

Viscosity is a central determinant of electrospinning jet stability because it controls the solution’s ability to elongate under the electric field [N5-R3]. The evidence shows that solution viscosity is directly tied to electrically driven jet elongation, and that higher viscosity generally resists stretching [N5-R3][N2-R1]. This is important because jet elongation is the process that turns the cone into a thin jet and ultimately determines fiber diameter.

Viscosity also influences charge accumulation and jet fragmentation. The review material explicitly states that rheology influences the nature of the fiber, morphology, and charge dynamics [N5-R3]. A more specific source on melt electrospinning notes that viscosity and electrical conductivity affect morphology and fiber diameter, reinforcing the idea that viscosity is part of the broader charge and breakup dynamics [N3-R3]. In practical terms, higher viscosity can suppress breakup and bead formation, but it can also reduce the jet’s ability to stretch sufficiently and may lead to less uniform fibers if the viscosity becomes too high [N2-R1][N5-R3][N3-R3].

### 3. Viscosity controls fiber diameter distribution and surface morphology

Viscosity strongly controls fiber diameter distribution and surface morphology. The evidence repeatedly links viscosity to diameter and morphology: molecular weight, alongside concentration and viscosity, is a predominant factor influencing morphology and diameter [N4-R4]; viscosity is a vital material parameter for electrospinning [N5-R3]; and the morphology of electrospun fibers is affected by solution properties including viscosity, conductivity, and surface tension [N5-R5]. Taken together, these sources support the conclusion that higher viscosity can produce more uniform fibers when the jet can still elongate sufficiently, while lower viscosity may produce wider diameter distributions or instability [N5-R3][N4-R4][N5-R5].

The evidence also implies that surface morphology is shaped by the same rheological controls. High surface tension can inhibit electrospinning and increase instability, leading to beaded fibers [N6-R3]. This means that viscosity interacts with surface tension to determine whether the jet forms beads or smooth fibers [N5-R5][N6-R3].

### 4. Electrical and surface properties add another layer of control

Electrical and surface properties are central to jet stability because they control charge buildup, jet breakup, and the final morphology [N5-R5][N6-R3]. Conductivity and surface tension influence charge buildup and stability. The evidence states that the morphology of electrospun fibers is affected by viscosity, conductivity, and surface tension [N5-R5]. It also notes that high surface tension inhibits electrospinning and increases instability, with the jet tending to break and form beads [N6-R3]. This supports the idea that surface tension suppresses jet stability by making the jet more prone to breakup, while conductivity affects how charge builds up and is released [N5-R5][N6-R3].

Electrical properties also affect the formation of beads and fiber uniformity. The evidence links conductivity and surface tension to fiber morphology and diameter [N5-R5]. High surface tension increases bead formation, and the review material states that the rheology of the spinning fluid greatly influences jet stability and morphology [N4-R1]. This means that when the electrical environment is unfavorable—such as when surface tension is high or conductivity is too low—the jet is less able to stretch smoothly and more likely to form beads [N5-R5][N6-R3][N4-R1].

Surface tension modifies jet breakup and fiber orientation. The evidence directly states that high surface tension inhibits electrospinning and increases the tendency for the jet to break, resulting in beaded fibers [N6-R3]. It also notes that the morphology of electrospun fibers is affected by surface tension, viscosity, and conductivity [N5-R5]. The review material further emphasizes that the rheology of the spinning fluid influences jet stability and morphology [N4-R1]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that surface tension can change the jet’s breakup behavior: lower surface tension favors elongation and smoother fibers, while higher surface tension favors instability and beading. The evidence does not provide a direct statement on fiber orientation, but it does support the broader conclusion that surface tension modifies the overall jet dynamics and morphology [N6-R3][N5-R5][N4-R1].

### 5. Combined effects: concentration, viscosity, and electrical properties interact

The combined effects of concentration, viscosity, and electrical properties are best understood as an interconnected system in which each parameter affects jet behavior, charge dynamics, and fiber morphology [N2-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5][N4-R1]. Concentration sets the baseline viscosity, which then interacts with electrical properties to determine how charge accumulates and how the jet fragments [N2-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5][N6-R3].

The evidence supports a coupled relationship: concentration controls viscosity, viscosity controls jet elongation and fragmentation, and electrical properties control charge buildup and breakup [N2-R1][N5-R3][N3-R3]. At the same time, surface tension modifies jet breakup and morphology, meaning that optimizing concentration alone is not sufficient; one must also consider solvent/additive choice and process parameters [N2-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

### 6. Practical implications for optimization

The practical implications are clear from the evidence. The review material states that the rheology of the spinning fluid greatly influences jet stability and morphology [N4-R1]. It also says that concentration and viscosity are among the dominant factors influencing fiber diameter and morphology [N4-R2][N4-R4]. A separate source notes that the morphology of electrospun fibers is affected by solution properties including viscosity, conductivity, and surface tension [N5-R5]. This means that process optimization must balance concentration to achieve the desired viscosity, solvent/additive choice to control surface tension and conductivity, and process parameters such as voltage, distance, and withdrawal rate to support stable jetting and uniform fiber formation [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R5].

The evidence also implies that additives can be used to tune viscosity and surface tension, which is important because higher polymer concentrations alone may not always produce the best morphology [N2-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5]. In other words, a successful electrospinning process is not just about choosing the right concentration; it is about choosing the right combination of polymer concentration, solvent/additive system, and process conditions so that the jet remains stable, elongates properly, and deposits into uniform nanofibers [N2-R1][N5-R3][N4-R1][N5-R5].

### 7. Bottom line

In short: concentration affects jet stability and morphology by setting solution viscosity and shifting the system between stable jetting, breakup, and dripping [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4]. Higher concentration increases viscosity and resistance to jet stretching, which can stabilize the jet initially but also make breakup more likely if viscosity becomes too high [N2-R1][N5-R3]. Viscosity controls elongation, charge accumulation, and fragmentation, and it strongly influences fiber diameter distribution and surface morphology [N5-R3][N3-R3][N5-R5]. Electrical and surface properties add another layer of control: conductivity affects charge buildup, while surface tension affects jet breakup and bead formation [N5-R5][N6-R3]. Together, these factors interact in a coupled way, so optimizing concentration, solvent/additive choice, and process parameters is essential for achieving stable jetting and the desired nanofiber morphology [N2-R1][N5-R3][N4-R1][N5-R5].
